clue.text: Are Trump rumours initially denied? Ask Stormy to prepare for battle

indicators.note: a stormy sea is churned up, so these letters are tossed into a new order
the letter picked is refused a place, so it is taken out of the words before it
the first letter of the next word is the one picked

explanation.surface: A query about whether a US president's rumours were denied, with a nod to Stormy Daniels and a call to battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' picks R from 'rumours' and 'denied' drops one R from ARETRUMP; 'Stormy' then shuffles the remaining AETRUMP with ASK. 'Stormy' looks like a name (Stormy Daniels) but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to take up weapons is to get ready to fight.

clue.text: Begin to grab raised tool … steady!

indicators.note: the first word seizes the other piece and holds it within itself

parts.note: to begin is to start

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: an awl is a pointed tool for piercing holes

explanation.surface: Someone told to pick up a tool and start work, then urged to hold it steady.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'raised' reads upwards, so the tool is reversed before 'to grab' takes it in. 'steady' looks like a command but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a stalwart supporter is firm, loyal and dependable.

clue.text: In posh jail, prisoner's beginning to unravel

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage, so posh

indicators.note: the picked letter is placed within the two pieces that follow in the clue

parts.note: nick is British slang for a prison or police station

indicators.note: the first letter of the word prisoner's is the one taken

explanation.surface: An upper-class prison where an inmate's plans begin to come apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' gives P, and 'In' puts it inside U + NICK, after the U. NICK is British slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to unpick stitching is to undo it thread by thread.

clue.text: Sartre's way very sound for philosopher

indicators.note: sound here means the letters are spoken, so what is heard counts, not the spelling

parts.note: Sartre wrote in French, where a way or street is rue; very is so

explanation.surface: A comment that Sartre's approach is very sound, said in praise of a philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sartre's' signals French: rue is a street. RUE + SO, said aloud, gives the name of the Geneva-born thinker. 'sound' looks like praise but is the homophone signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was the 18th-century Enlightenment thinker who wrote The Social Contract.

clue.text: Polish official in East

parts.note: a referee, or ref, is a sports official
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A Polish official working somewhere in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like a nationality but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to polish something is to improve and perfect it.

clue.text: Quick, there's no time — run!

indicators.note: says the letter for time is absent, so it comes out of the word for quick

parts.note: fleet means fast or quick

explanation.surface: An urgent warning: no time left, so run for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there's no' removes T from FLEET.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to flee is to run away from danger.

clue.text: Doctor screened patient Irish leader

parts.note: Doc Martin is a British TV drama about a grumpy Cornish GP, so the doctor shown on screen is Martin
a patient is one who is ill

explanation.surface: A TV doctor treating a patient who turns out to be an Irish politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish leader' suggests a taoiseach, but the answer is the football manager who led the Republic of Ireland team (2013-18).
explanation.definitionFit: Martin O'Neill managed the Republic of Ireland national football side, so he led Ireland.

clue.text: See 7
Path to war? Say, put a lid on it!

indicators.note: letters sent to war are thrown into disorder, so the word path is rearranged

parts.note: e.g. means for example, which say also means

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a path leads to war and is told to keep quiet about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to war' rearranges PATH into HATP. 'put a lid on it' looks like 'be quiet', but a lid is slang for a hat, and you put a hat on this.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic sense: a peg on which you hang a hat, slang lid, is what you put a lid on.

clue.text: Raised north-east favourite some way from here

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: Rafa Benitez was a popular manager of Newcastle United, in the north-east of England

explanation.surface: A favourite from the north-east has moved some distance away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' turns RAFA round. 'north-east' suggests NE, but it locates the favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something afar is at a distance, a long way off.

clue.text: Referring to space on one side of Madrid

parts.note: a is the indefinite article, meaning one
Real Madrid is a Spanish football team, a side

explanation.surface: A remark about space down one flank of a football pitch in Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'space' suggests the open pitch, but the definition is about area.
explanation.definitionFit: Areal is the adjective of area, describing extent of a surface.

clue.text: Fancy top is fine for all

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or made up, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An elaborate shirt suits every wearer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for all' is used as in 'for all his faults', meaning notwithstanding.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym phrase: 'for all' and 'despite' both concede a point while maintaining the opposite.

clue.text: City big shot on track with no small encouragement

parts.note: Pep Guardiola is the celebrated manager of Manchester City

indicators.note: says the letter for small is dropped from the word for track

parts.note: to stalk prey is to track it

explanation.surface: A city's big shot out on the track giving a little encouragement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes S from STALK. 'City' is Manchester City football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a rousing speech to raise morale is a form of encouragement.

clue.text: Flat race without a horse

parts.note: a flat surface is even

indicators.note: the letter A is removed from the word for race

parts.note: to tear is to race or rush along

explanation.surface: A flat race held with no horse in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops A from TEAR, leaving TER. 'Flat race' looks like a horse-racing term, but Flat gives EVEN and race gives TEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: an eventer is a horse trained for the three-discipline sport of eventing.

clue.text: Ground bare — resite plants

indicators.note: ground means crushed or milled, so the letters are broken up and remixed

explanation.surface: A gardener instructs that, the soil being bare, plants be moved elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like soil but is the past tense of grind, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Teaberries are wintergreen shrubs, low-growing evergreen plants with red fruit.

clue.text: Oxford principal taught Greats — he could be boss

indicators.note: says the letters that come before might be turned into something else, a rearrangement
the principal or chief letter of Oxford is its first

explanation.surface: An Oxford college head who taught Classics might one day run the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principal' gives O, which 'could be' shuffles with TAUGHTGREATSHE. Greats is the Oxford name for its Classics degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Gareth Southgate was England's football manager, the boss of the national team.

clue.text: Home counties toff was all over doctor

indicators.note: says everything before it is turned over, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: the Home Counties around London are in the south-east, SE
a nob is a British upper-class person, a toff

explanation.surface: A Home Counties toff who once ran all over the place is now a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all over' turns SENOBWAS round. The Home Counties are the counties around London.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones is an old slang term for a surgeon or physician.

clue.text: Trying to travel free from Hertfordshire town to Gateshead

parts.note: Hitchin is a market town in Hertfordshire, England
read as gate's head, the first letter of gate

explanation.surface: Thumbing a lift all the way from Hitchin in Hertfordshire to Gateshead on Tyneside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gateshead' looks like the Tyneside town but is split as gate's head, giving G.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to hitch a ride is to get a free lift from passing drivers.

clue.text: Extremely naughty poem about Don Juan, perhaps

indicators.note: about means round and about, so these letters are scattered into a new order
the extreme letters of naughty are its first and last

explanation.surface: A very rude poem about the notorious seducer Don Juan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' gives NY, and 'about' shuffles NY with POEM. Byron's Don Juan is a poem, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Don Juan's name came to mean a womaniser, so he lends his name to a word.

clue.text: Lie scattered on top — were nearly knocked over

parts.note: to top is to beat, as is to best

indicators.note: knocked over means toppled, so the letters are turned round
nearly means not quite all, so the last letter of were is dropped

explanation.surface: Things lying scattered on top that were almost knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' cuts WERE to WER, and 'knocked over' turns it into REW.
explanation.definitionFit: Bestrew is a literary verb meaning to be strewn or scattered over a surface.

clue.text: Attempt to keep new tie

indicators.note: the word for attempt holds the other letter within itself

parts.note: a bid is an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone tries to keep a new necktie in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tie' looks like the noun for neckwear in the surface but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to bind something is to fasten it with cord or rope.

clue.text: Recited Frost's poetry

indicators.note: recited means said aloud, so the spoken form counts, not the spelling

parts.note: rime is hoar frost, so frosts are rimes

explanation.surface: Someone recites the poems of Robert Frost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frost' looks like the poet Robert Frost but means rime, the ice crystals.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: rhymes are verses, a general term for poetry.

clue.text: About town, Henry and I are active

parts.note: on can mean about, as in a talk on a subject
T is an abbreviation for town
H is the symbol for the henry, the SI unit of inductance
ego is the Latin for I, the self

explanation.surface: Henry and I are out about town, being busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' looks like a friend's name but is the unit of inductance, H.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: someone constantly busy and moving about is always active.

clue.text: Punches to face ultimately won't hurt

indicators.note: hurt means damaged, so these letters are knocked out of shape
the final letters of the words to and face are the ones taken

explanation.surface: A boxer's reassurance that blows to the face won't hurt in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives O and E, and 'hurt' shuffles them with WONT.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxing term: two quick blows in succession, left then right, form a combination of punches.

clue.text: Run away from land — one's that's special in your dreams

indicators.note: the letter for run is taken away from the country's name

parts.note: Norway is a land, a country
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
José Mourinho styled himself the Special One

explanation.surface: A dreamer runs away from a country to someone special.
explanation.walkthrough: 'away from' removes R from NORWAY. José Mourinho called himself 'the Special One' when he joined Chelsea.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: both phrases are mocking refusals, saying something will never happen.

clue.text: Was in a bit of bother, owning up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters are read bottom to top
the letters sit within the run of words that follows, a piece of them

explanation.surface: Someone in a bit of trouble, confessing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of' finds EROW across 'bother, owning', and 'up' turns it round. 'owning up' looks like a phrase, but only 'up' is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: if you wore a coat, you were in it, dressed in it.

clue.text: He managed to worry

definitions.meaning: ... Redknapp, the football manager of Spurs and others
to harass or pester someone persistently

explanation.surface: A manager remembered for causing worry.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Redknapp managed Tottenham and other clubs; to harry is to harass or worry.

clue.text: Long server behind Greens — one's confused

parts.note: arse is British slang for the backside or behind
two words for green: new, as in inexperienced, is the first

indicators.note: says one of the two greens has its letters jumbled

parts.note: the second of the two greens is the colour word itself

explanation.surface: A long-serving figure behind the Greens, one of whom is muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greens' supplies two greens: NEW, and GREEN which 'one's confused' rearranges to ENGER. ARSE is British slang for the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsène Wenger managed Arsenal for 22 years, serving a long tenure.

clue.text: See 26
